blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Not all facts a language model can recall support further learning equally well. We distinguish active facts, which support generalization beyond their own recall, from inert facts, which can be recalled but do not support such generalization in a given task. We study this distinction by constructing new relations from existing ones. Take the relation that maps a place to its continent (Paris -> Europe) and assign each of its answers an arbitrary new label (Europe -> crab, Asia -> zebra). The new relation then maps Paris -> crab. We fine-tune the model on the new relation for a subset of subjects, without telling it the original relation or the relabeling rule, and test whether it assigns the corresponding labels to held-out subjects that share an answer in the original relation. Having learned Paris -> crab, does it answer Munich -> crab? Across eleven language models and 70 relations, how linearly readable the original relation is in pretrained representations strongly predicts this generalization. Within each model, the two correlate across relations at Pearson r = 0.87 to 0.92. This association persists when controlling, separately and jointly, for the number of fine-tuning subjects and answers, the model's accuracy on the original relation, and how often the subjects occur in pretraining text. It is also robust to re-randomizing the label assignment and fine-tuning seed, and to replacing the animal labels with labels from thirteen other semantic categories. When we map a fine-tuned model's wrong label back to the original answer it was assigned to, Munich -> zebra becomes Munich -> Asia. Answers recovered this way are more often among the linear probe's top answers for the subject than among the pretrained model's own. Whether a new relation generalizes depends less on whether its facts can be recalled than on how readily their shared structure can be read out linearly.

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
Imagine that the pretraining text describes Mary as having grown up in France,
attending French schools, writing books in French and working in French-speaking
institutions, but never states her native language. A language model should
still assume that Mary is a native speaker of French. We call this statistical generalization of facts . The model infers a new fact from
facts it knows, by a statistical rule that the pretraining text rarely states
explicitly and that is not always true. It differs from entailment, where the new
fact follows necessarily from the known ones, and from paraphrase, where the
same fact is merely worded differently ( Section 2 ). Statistical
generalization is a large part of what makes language models useful beyond
recalling what they were told. Prior work has asked whether models draw such
inferences from facts they are trained on ( Feng et al., 2025 ; Treutlein et al., 2024 ) ,
but, to our
knowledge, no prior work has asked which of a model’s facts support them.

We hypothesize that the answer is linear structure. Linear relational
embeddings were originally proposed as a mechanism for generalizing to unseen
relational facts ( Paccanaro & Hinton, 2000 ) , and many relations in
modern language models are, to a good approximation, decoded linearly from the
subject’s representation ( Hernandez et al., 2024 ; Merullo et al., 2025 ) . In a
synthetic setting, knowledge that is linearly encoded on the entity is the
knowledge that fine-tuning can extract ( Allen-Zhu & Li, 2024 ) . But
whether the linearity of a pretrained model’s real-world knowledge affects how new knowledge built on it generalizes has not been
tested.
The hypothesis we investigate is that the more linearly readable a relation’s
answers are in the pretrained model, which we call the relation’s Pre-linearity , the better new knowledge built on that relation
generalizes after fine-tuning.

To this end, we construct new relations from existing ones

continent (Paris → \to Europe) and relabel each of its answers at random with
a different arbitrary word, such as an animal name (Europe → \to crab, Asia → \to zebra). The resulting new relation maps Paris → \to crab. We fine-tune the model
on the new relation for a subset of subjects, without telling it the original
relation or the relabeling rule, and test whether it assigns the right labels to
held-out subjects. Having learned Paris → \to crab, does it answer Munich → \to crab? The design directly tests for statistical generalization. The new relation is
unknown to the model, but its structure is inherited from the
pretrained relation, so the model can generalize only by building on what it already

pretrained model’s subject representations, Recall as the
pretrained model’s accuracy on the pretrained relation, and Generalization as the
fine-tuned model’s accuracy on held-out subjects
( Section 3 ).

Our contributions are: (1) We introduce the distinction between active and inert facts, and a

relation size and subject frequency are controlled for jointly.
Furthermore,
the probe predicts the fine-tuned models’ errors better
than the other explanations we test.

blocks.en:
Most related to our distinction between
inert vs active facts is work on inference from facts that
we will call “entailment.” A fact f f is entailed
by a set of other facts F F if from accepting the truth of F F , it
necessarily follows that the truth of f f has to be
accepted. For example,
{“John lives in Tokyo”, “Tokyo is in Japan”, “People in Japan speak
Japanese”} entails “Where John lives, people speak Japanese” ( Feng et al., 2025 ) .
This type of entailment includes transitive inference,
inverse relations and kinship reasoning and it
has
been widely studied ( Berglund et al., 2024 ; Mehrafarin et al., 2024 ; Efeoglu & Paschke, 2026 ; Fesser et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2024 ; Lampinen et al., 2025 , e.g.,) .
There is mixed evidence on how well LMs perform on
entailment ( Talmor et al., 2020 ; Clark et al., 2021 ) .

It is investigated by Lu et al. (2024) , but their focus is

undesirable. Many authors make the implicit
assumption that language models should not say something
that has not been stated in the pretraining data (modulo the
cases of entailment and paraphrasing discussed above),
even if it is mathematically unavoidable ( Kalai et al., 2025 ) .
This assumption may be misguided. Part of the
effectiveness of language models is that they perform
statistical generalization and operate on statistical
inferences that are not guaranteed to be true 100%.

blocks.en:
In summary, there is much work on entailment, factual recall and
linguistic generalization, but, to our knowledge, the
question of which known facts a model can build new
facts on has not been addressed.
We address it in a fine-tuning setting and find that
whether facts are active, that is, whether new relations
built on them generalize, is predicted better by how
linearly readable they are before fine-tuning than by
whether the model can recall them.
This sheds light on how facts are represented in
language models and how this representation supports
learning and generalization.

blocks.en: Appendix B Fine-tuning recipe
blocks.zh: 附录B 微调配方

blocks.en:
Every model is fine-tuned with the same recipe, on all of its parameters.
A relation has 4 ​ | T | 4\lvert T\rvert training records, one per
fine-tuning subject and template pair.
A record is the prompt followed by a space and the label, and the loss is the
cross-entropy at the label’s first token only.
The optimizer is AdamW with β = ( 0.9 , 0.95 ) \beta=(0.9,0.95) , ϵ = 10 − 8 \epsilon=10^{-8} and no
weight decay, and gradients are clipped to norm 1.0 1.0 .
The learning rate warms up linearly to 10 − 5 10^{-5} over the first 10% of steps
and then decays along a cosine to 10 − 6 10^{-6} .
Each step averages the gradient over 16 records.
We run micro-batches of 4 records per device (2 for Gemma-4-E2B and
Qwen3.8-27B) with gradient accumulation, and shard models that need more than
one GPU with fully sharded data parallelism, on up to eight GPUs.
Training runs for 20 epochs, each using every record once in a fresh order, so
every fine-tuning fact is seen 80 times, 20 in each wording.
Forward and backward passes run in bfloat16; the parameters and the AdamW
moments are kept in float32.
Generalization is read after the last epoch.
Subject roles, the label subset L L and the folds use one fixed seed in every
run; the bijection is keyed by relation and repetition, and the optimizer
seed, which also sets the record order, equals the repetition index. Table 3 gives each model’s accuracy on its fine-tuning
subjects after the last epoch.

blocks.en:
A name of the category is kept only if
(i) its primary sense lies under the category’s root synset
( animal.n.01 for animals), so the new-relation prompt’s request for
“one animal” is true of it;
(ii) no other kept name is its hyponym, so each prompt has one correct label;
(iii) it is common in English, with wordfreq zipf frequency at least
2.32;
(iv) its first token differs from every other kept name’s under the tokenizer
of every model the label set is used with, since we score only first
tokens; and
(v) the cosine between its first token’s unembedding row and any other kept
name’s is at most 0.446 under MiniCPM5-2B-Base .
For each pretrained relation R R , the draw of L L then excludes every name that equals a
subject or answer of R R , or whose primary sense lies within
four WordNet hypernym steps of one, so that no label is a
taxonomic neighbor of R R ’s subjects or answers ( neighbor pruning ).

Several explanations can point at the same wrong answer. The error is then shared: each explanation
that accounts for it gets an equal part. This is the Shapley value of the game in which a set of
explanations is worth the number of errors that at least one of them accounts for. An error that no
explanation accounts for is unexplained. An explanation’s share is its credit divided by the number
of errors, pooled over all fine-tuned models, so the shares and the unexplained rest sum to 100%.

blocks.en:
An explanation can match a wrong answer by coincidence, and the two baselines measure how often. The
shuffled baseline takes the wrong answers one fine-tuned model gave and hands them out again among
its errors at random. In expectation, each error receives each of those answers, its own included,
with equal probability. An answer equal to the error’s correct answer is skipped, since it would not
be an error. This keeps the model’s preference for some wrong labels and breaks only their link to
the subject. The chance baseline instead gives each error a uniformly random wrong label: any label
of its new relation except the correct one. Both baselines are computed exactly as expectations, not by
sampling.

是一个错误。 这保持了模型对一些错误标签的偏好,并且只打破它们与
主题。 相反,机会基线给每个错误一个统一随机的错误标签:任何标签
除了正确的关系之外 这两项基准的计算完全按照预期进行,而不是按照
取样。

blocks.en:
The most frequent answer is the one explanation the shuffle cannot test. It points at the same
answer for every held-out subject of a fine-tuned model, so the number of wrong answers that equal
it does not depend on which subject gave which answer. Shuffling leaves that number almost
unchanged. Its shuffled share even rises, to 6.1% from
5.0% observed, because the other explanations match less often after
the shuffle and leave it a larger part of the credit. Against chance
(1.9%), the most frequent answer does account for more errors than
coincidence.
